title: Neural Tree Collaborative Filtering: Rethinking Graph Collaborative Filtering as Tree Collaborative Filtering with Curvature-Aware Propagation Depth

paper.title: Neural Tree Collaborative Filtering: Rethinking Graph Collaborative Filtering as Tree Collaborative Filtering with Curvature-Aware Propagation Depth
paper.abstract: Abstract. Graph Collaborative Filtering (GCF) has become the dominant paradigm in modern recommender systems by modeling user--item interactions as a bipartite graph and propagating embeddings through a fixed number of message-passing layers. However, applying a uniform propagation depth to every node ignores a fundamental property of real interaction graphs: nodes differ substantially in their local connectivity, so peripheral nodes quickly suffer from over-smoothing while hub-like nodes remain under-explored beyond their immediate neighborhood. In this paper, we revisit GCF from a tree-structured perspective and propose Neural Tree Collaborative Filtering (NTCF), a framework that re-interprets each node’s local neighborhood as a rooted tree and assigns a node-specific propagation depth based on a closed-form local-degree-imbalance score that serves as a discrete Ricci-curvature proxy. We provide a theoretical analysis showing that (i) NTCF strictly generalizes NGCF, degenerating to NGCF when all curvature-induced depth adjustments vanish (a lower bound on its representation power), and (ii) the curvature-aware schedule retains strictly more discriminative information at deep layers on positively-curved (peripheral) nodes than uniform-depth propagation. NTCF can achieve higher performance than most widely used GCF backbone models and can be integrated into existing advanced self-supervised models as a backbone, replacing their original backbone to achieve enhanced performance. Extensive experiments on three public datasets demonstrate the superiority of NTCF 1 1 1 Code is available at: https://github.com/Jinfeng-Xu/NTCF . .

sections.heading: 1. Introduction
sections.text: Recommender systems are widely used to alleviate information overload on the Web ( Xu et al., 2025c ; He et al., 2017 ; Xu et al., 2024 ; Xu et al., 2025d ) . Collaborative Filtering (CF) addresses the recommendation problem by learning user preferences from historical interactions of similar users. Recently, Graph Collaborative Filtering (GCF) ( Wang et al., 2019 ; Xu et al., 2026a ; Chen et al., 2025b ; He et al., 2020 ; Liu et al., 2021 ; Mao et al., 2021 ; Chen et al., 2020 ) has become the dominant paradigm because the user-item interaction data is naturally graph-structured. Representative models such as NGCF ( Wang et al., 2019 ) adopt vanilla GCN architectures with feature transformation and nonlinear activation, while LightGCN ( He et al., 2020 ) simplifies these components and has since served as the backbone of many follow-up GCF and self-supervised models ( Yu et al., 2022 ; Xu et al., 2025b ; Chen et al., 2025a ; Zhang et al., 2024 ; Lin et al., 2022 ) . Despite its empirical success, the prevailing GCF paradigm shares a structural limitation that has received little attention: every node propagates information through exactly the same number of layers L L . From the perspective of each individual node, message passing can be viewed as constructing a rooted tree of depth L L in which the node itself is the root and its (multi-hop) neighbors form the descendants. Forcing this tree to have the same depth for all nodes is, in fact, unnatural. Real user-item interaction graphs are highly heterogeneous: peripheral nodes whose neighbors are dense local hubs see information that is already heavily mixed at one or two hops away, so deepening their tree merely re-aggregates over-smoothed signals ( Chen et al., 2020 ; Zhao and Akoglu, 2020 ; Liu et al., 2020 ) ; in contrast, locally-hub-like nodes whose immediate neighbors are themselves comparatively peripheral need deeper exploration to reach the informative collaborative signals that lie beyond their immediate neighborhood. This observation prompts a question that lies at the heart of GCF design: should the propagation depth be a node-level property rather than a global hyper-parameter? If propagation can be made node-adaptive while preserving the bidirectional nature of the user-item graph, GCF can in principle be re-interpreted as an ensemble of node-rooted trees, with each tree’s depth tailored to the local geometry of the graph at its root. Motivated by this perspective, we propose Neural Tree Collaborative Filtering (NTCF) . NTCF re-interprets the bipartite interaction graph as a collection of rooted trees, one per node, in which message passing fills the tree from the root outwards. Crucially, the depth of each tree is no longer a global hyper-parameter but is determined by a closed-form, O ⁡ ( | ℰ | ) O(|\mathcal{E}|) -computable local degree-imbalance score that serves as a discrete-Ricci-curvature proxy ( Ollivier, 2009 ; Lin et al., 2011 ) . The score provides a principled, data-driven measure of how a node’s local connectivity compares to that of its neighbors, and translates directly into a node-specific depth: negative-curvature local hubs receive a deeper tree to reach far collaborative signals, positive-curvature peripheral nodes receive a shallower tree to avoid re-aggregating already-mixed signals, and curvature-flat nodes keep the standard depth. Because this scheme reduces to standard NGCF propagation when no node receives a curvature adjustment, NTCF provably contains NGCF as a special case while admitting a broader family of node-adaptive propagation patterns.

sections.heading: 2.2. Tree-Structured View of GCF
sections.text: A useful but underexplored fact about Eq. 1 is that, from the standpoint of any single node v v , L L -layer GCN propagation produces an embedding that depends only on the rooted tree obtained by unrolling 𝒢 \mathcal{G} around v v to depth L L . We formalize this tree as follows. Definition 0 (Rooted Propagation Tree). For a node v ∈ 𝒱 v\in\mathcal{V} and depth L ∈ ℕ L\in\mathbb{N} , the rooted propagation tree 𝒯 v ( L ) \mathcal{T}_{v}^{(L)} is defined by breadth-first unrolling of 𝒢 \mathcal{G} from v v for L L hops. Each node in 𝒯 v ( L ) \mathcal{T}_{v}^{(L)} corresponds to a walk of length at most L L originating at v v , and edges follow the bipartite structure of 𝒢 \mathcal{G} . Under this view, GCN-style propagation can be equivalently described as: for every v ∈ 𝒱 v\in\mathcal{V} , build 𝒯 v ( L ) \mathcal{T}_{v}^{(L)} and aggregate information from leaves to root. This makes explicit the fact that NGCF and its successors implicitly assume the same tree depth L L for every node —a global hyper-parameter that ignores the heterogeneous local geometry of 𝒢 \mathcal{G} . We relax this assumption by allowing each node to have its own depth L v L_{v} , and we use a closed-form local-curvature score (Sec. 2.3 ) to determine L v L_{v} .

sections.heading: 2.3. Local Degree-Imbalance Curvature on Graphs
sections.text: Discrete-graph analogues of Ricci curvature, such as Ollivier-Ricci curvature ( Ollivier, 2009 ) and the Lin-Lu-Yau ( Lin et al., 2011 ) variant, characterize how a node’s local connectivity compares to that of its neighbors. Exact computation of these quantities, however, requires solving an optimal-transport problem at every edge, which is impractical for industrial-scale interaction graphs containing millions of edges. We therefore adopt a simple, closed-form curvature proxy that captures the same local-imbalance intuition while admitting an O ⁡ ( | ℰ | ) O(|\mathcal{E}|) pre-computation. Given a node v v with degree d ⁡ ( v ) d(v) , we define its local degree-imbalance score κ ⁡ ( v ) \kappa(v) as: (2) κ ⁡ ( v ) = d ¯ 𝒩 ⁡ ( v ) − d ⁡ ( v ) d ¯ 𝒩 ⁡ ( v ) + d ⁡ ( v ) + ϵ , \kappa(v)\;=\;\frac{\bar{d}_{\mathcal{N}(v)}-d(v)}{\bar{d}_{\mathcal{N}(v)}+d(v)+\epsilon}, where d ¯ 𝒩 ⁡ ( v ) = 1 | 𝒩 ⁡ ( v ) | ​ ∑ w ∈ 𝒩 ⁡ ( v ) d ⁡ ( w ) \bar{d}_{\mathcal{N}(v)}=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{N}(v)|}\sum_{w\in\mathcal{N}(v)}d(w) is the average degree of v v ’s neighbors and ϵ > 0 \epsilon>0 avoids division by zero. The interpretation is intuitive. When d ⁡ ( v ) > d ¯ 𝒩 ⁡ ( v ) d(v)>\bar{d}_{\mathcal{N}(v)} , the node is itself more connected than its neighbors and κ ⁡ ( v ) < 0 \kappa(v)<0 : v v acts as a local hub whose neighbors are comparatively peripheral, so a deeper propagation tree can reach informative two- or three-hop signals that a shallow tree would miss. When d ⁡ ( v ) < d ¯ 𝒩 ⁡ ( v ) d(v)<\bar{d}_{\mathcal{N}(v)} , the node sits at the periphery of a more densely connected local cluster and κ ⁡ ( v ) > 0 \kappa(v)>0 : deepening the tree merely re-aggregates information that is already heavily mixed in the local hub, accelerating over-smoothing, so a shallower tree is preferable. When κ ⁡ ( v ) ≈ 0 \kappa(v)\!\approx\!0 , the node and its neighbors are comparably connected and the standard depth is appropriate. Eq. 2 is bounded in [ − 1 , 1 ] [-1,1] and is computed once at preprocessing time. For brevity, we simply refer to κ ⁡ ( v ) \kappa(v) as the curvature of v v in the rest of the paper.

sections.heading: Complexity.
sections.text: The curvature pre-computation in Eq. 3 costs O ⁡ ( | ℰ | ) O(|\mathcal{E}|) and is performed once and cached. Each training epoch shares the same per-layer sparse-aggregation cost as NGCF, O ⁡ ( L max ⋅ | ℰ | ⋅ d ) O(L_{\max}\!\cdot\!|\mathcal{E}|\!\cdot\!d) , plus a negligible O ⁡ ( | 𝒱 | ⋅ d ) O(|\mathcal{V}|\!\cdot\!d) masking step per layer. Since L max ≤ L + 1 L_{\max}\!\leq\!L\!+\!1 , NTCF’s training cost exceeds NGCF’s by at most a single message-passing layer, with no recurring overhead from the cached curvature.

sections.heading: 4.1. Datasets and Evaluation Metrics
sections.text: To validate NTCF, we experiment on three public datasets: Yelp ( Xu et al., 2025e ) , Amazon Kindle store ( He and McAuley, 2016 ) , and Pinterest ( Geng et al., 2015 ) . They vary in scale and sparsity. For Yelp we use a 15-core setting (minimum 15 interactions), and for Kindle and Pinterest we filter out users and items with fewer than 5 interactions. Following prior works ( Lin et al., 2022 ; Zhang et al., 2024 ; Xu et al., 2025a ; Chen et al., 2025b ) , we adopt a user-based split with training, validation, and test sets in an : : 1 8\!:\!1\!:\!1 ratio. We report two established metrics ( He et al., 2020 ) : Recall@ K K (R@ K K ) and NDCG@ K K (N@ K K ) for K ∈ { 10 , 20 , 50 } K\in\{10,20,50\} . All results are averaged over 5 5 runs with different seeds.

sections.heading: 4.2. Baselines and Experimental Settings
sections.text: To verify the effectiveness of our NTCF, we compare it with six widely used GCN-based backbone models: NCF ( He et al., 2017 ) , NGCF ( Wang et al., 2019 ) , LightGCN ( He et al., 2020 ) , UltraGCN ( Mao et al., 2021 ) , IMP-GCN ( Liu et al., 2021 ) , and FKAN-GCF ( Xu et al., 2025a ) . Moreover, to verify NTCF’s compatibility with self-supervised methods, we replace the original LightGCN backbone of four advanced self-supervised models with NTCF: SimGCL ( Yu et al., 2022 ) , LightGCL ( Cai et al., 2023 ) , RecDCL ( Zhang et al., 2024 ) , and NLGCL ( Xu et al., 2025e ; Xu et al., 2026b ) . For a fair comparison, we fix the embedding size to 64 64 for all models, initialize embeddings with Xavier initialization ( Glorot and Bengio, 2010 ) , and use Adam ( Kingma and Ba, 2014 ) as the optimizer. Hyper-parameters of all baselines are tuned following their published papers. For NTCF, we fix λ = 10 − 4 \lambda=10^{-4} , tune the layer number L L from { 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 } \{1,2,3,4\} , the curvature threshold τ \tau from { 0.05 , 0.1 , 0.2 , 0.4 } \{0.05,0.1,0.2,0.4\} , and the message dropout ratio from { 0.0 , 0.1 , 0.2 , 0.3 } \{0.0,0.1,0.2,0.3\} .

sections.heading: 4.3. Performance Comparison
sections.text: The results are reported in Table 1 . NTCF consistently outperforms all baselines on both metrics across all three datasets, which we attribute to curvature-aware propagation: peripheral nodes are spared late-layer over-smoothing, while hub nodes absorb farther collaborative signals. Its only overhead over NGCF is the per-node curvature score, computed once in O ⁡ ( | ℰ | ) O(|\mathcal{E}|) and cached.

sections.heading: 4.4. Compatibility Analysis
sections.text: We further evaluate the compatibility of NTCF with advanced self-supervised graph-based recommenders by replacing their default LightGCN backbones with NTCF. As shown in Table 2 , all four self-supervised methods (SimGCL, LightGCL, RecDCL, and NLGCL) consistently benefit from NTCF on every dataset and metric. This confirms that adapting propagation depth to the local geometry of each node is a property combinable with self-supervised contrastive objectives, and that NTCF can be deployed as a drop-in backbone improvement for the modern SSL-based recommendation pipeline.

sections.text: Table 1 also reports two ablations. w/o curvature sets τ → ∞ \tau\!\to\!\infty so that Δ ⁡ ( v ) ≡ 0 \Delta(v)\!\equiv\!0 for all nodes, recovering the NGCF-equivalent of NTCF predicted by Proposition 1 . r/ mean agg. replaces concatenation with the curvature-weighted mean aggregation in Eq. 6 . The curvature-aware variant outperforms the uniform-depth variant on all datasets, empirically corroborating the strict-improvement direction predicted by Proposition 2 , and concatenation slightly outperforms mean aggregation, justifying its use as the default.

sections.heading: 4.6. Hyper-parameter Analysis
sections.text: Figure 2 reports Recall@20 as we vary the base depth L L , the curvature threshold τ \tau , and the dropout ratio. The optimum is consistent across all three datasets: L = 3 L=3 , τ = 0.1 \tau=0.1 , and dropout = 0.2 =0.2 . NTCF prefers a moderate L L (consistent with prior GCF observations ( He et al., 2020 ; Wang et al., 2019 ) ); deeper stacks ( L = 4 L=4 ) start to over-smooth, while a shallow L = 1 L=1 removes the very signal NTCF is built to refine. A small but non-zero τ \tau is preferred: τ = 0.1 \tau\!=\!0.1 keeps a non-trivial fraction of nodes in the curvature-adjusted regime, whereas τ = 0.4 \tau\!=\!0.4 collapses NTCF toward NGCF and degrades performance. Performance varies by less than 0.5 0.5 percentage points (in absolute Recall@20) in a neighborhood of each optimum, indicating that NTCF is robust to hyper-parameter choice. Figure 2 . sections.heading: 5. Conclusion
sections.text: In this paper, we revisit the structural assumptions of graph collaborative filtering and identify that fixing a global propagation depth ignores the heterogeneous local geometry of real user–item graphs. Motivated by this observation, we propose Neural Tree Collaborative Filtering (NTCF), which reinterprets each node’s neighborhood as a rooted tree and assigns a node-specific propagation depth based on a closed-form local-degree-imbalance curvature score. We theoretically prove that NTCF strictly generalizes NGCF, degenerating to NGCF in the zero-adjustment limit (lower bound), and that, under the same Lipschitz contraction assumption used to analyze over-smoothing, NTCF maintains a non-vanishing Dirichlet-energy floor that uniform-depth NGCF provably loses as L L grows. Extensive experiments on three real-world datasets verify that NTCF consistently outperforms widely used GCF backbones and further boosts state-of-the-art self-supervised recommenders when used as their backbone. We hope this motivates further work on geometry-aware, node-adaptive message-passing schedules for GCF. Acknowledgements. Graph Collaborative Filtering (GCF) has become the dominant paradigm in modern recommender systems by modeling user--item interactions as a bipartite graph and propagating embeddings through a fixed number of message-passing layers. However, applying a uniform propagation depth to every node ignores a fundamental property of real interaction graphs: nodes differ substantially in their local connectivity, so peripheral nodes quickly suffer from over-smoothing while hub-like nodes remain under-explored beyond their immediate neighborhood. In this paper, we revisit GCF from a tree-structured perspective and propose Neural Tree Collaborative Filtering (NTCF), a framework that re-interprets each node’s local neighborhood as a rooted tree and assigns a node-specific propagation depth based on a closed-form local-degree-imbalance score that serves as a discrete Ricci-curvature proxy. We provide a theoretical analysis showing that (i) NTCF strictly generalizes NGCF, degenerating to NGCF when all curvature-induced depth adjustments vanish (a lower bound on its representation power), and (ii) the curvature-aware schedule retains strictly more discriminative information at deep layers on positively-curved (peripheral) nodes than uniform-depth propagation. NTCF can achieve higher performance than most widely used GCF backbone models and can be integrated into existing advanced self-supervised models as a backbone, replacing their original backbone to achieve enhanced performance. Extensive experiments on three public datasets demonstrate the superiority of NTCF 1 1 1 Code is available at: https://github.com/Jinfeng-Xu/NTCF . . Keywords: Recommender System, Graph Collaborative Filtering, Tree-Structured Propagation, Curvature-Aware Propagation † † cc-license: by 1. Introduction Recommender systems are widely used to alleviate information overload on the Web ( Xu et al., 2025c ; He et al., 2017 ; Xu et al., 2024 ; Xu et al., 2025d ) . Collaborative Filtering (CF) addresses the recommendation problem by learning user preferences from historical interactions of similar users. Recently, Graph Collaborative Filtering (GCF) ( Wang et al., 2019 ; Xu et al., 2026a ; Chen et al., 2025b ; He et al., 2020 ; Liu et al., 2021 ; Mao et al., 2021 ; Chen et al., 2020 ) has become the dominant paradigm because the user-item interaction data is naturally graph-structured. Representative models such as NGCF ( Wang et al., 2019 ) adopt vanilla GCN architectures with feature transformation and nonlinear activation, while LightGCN ( He et al., 2020 ) simplifies these components and has since served as the backbone of many follow-up GCF and self-supervised models ( Yu et al., 2022 ; Xu et al., 2025b ; Chen et al., 2025a ; Zhang et al., 2024 ; Lin et al., 2022 ) . Despite its empirical success, the prevailing GCF paradigm shares a structural limitation that has received little attention: every node propagates information through exactly the same number of layers L L . From the perspective of each individual node, message passing can be viewed as constructing a rooted tree of depth L L in which the node itself is the root and its (multi-hop) neighbors form the descendants. Forcing this tree to have the same depth for all nodes is, in fact, unnatural. Real user-item interaction graphs are highly heterogeneous: peripheral nodes whose neighbors are dense local hubs see information that is already heavily mixed at one or two hops away, so deepening their tree merely re-aggregates over-smoothed signals ( Chen et al., 2020 ; Zhao and Akoglu, 2020 ; Liu et al., 2020 ) ; in contrast, locally-hub-like nodes whose immediate neighbors are themselves comparatively peripheral need deeper exploration to reach the informative collaborative signals that lie beyond their immediate neighborhood. This observation prompts a question that lies at the heart of GCF design: should the propagation depth be a node-level property rather than a global hyper-parameter? If propagation can be made node-adaptive while preserving the bidirectional nature of the user-item graph, GCF can in principle be re-interpreted as an ensemble of node-rooted trees, with each tree’s depth tailored to the local geometry of the graph at its root. Motivated by this perspective, we propose Neural Tree Collaborative Filtering (NTCF) . NTCF re-interprets the bipartite interaction graph as a collection of rooted trees, one per node, in which message passing fills the tree from the root outwards. Crucially, the depth of each tree is no longer a global hyper-parameter but is determined by a closed-form, O ⁡ ( | ℰ | ) O(|\mathcal{E}|) -computable local degree-imbalance score that serves as a discrete-Ricci-curvature proxy ( Ollivier, 2009 ; Lin et al., 2011 ) . The score provides a principled, data-driven measure of how a node’s local connectivity compares to that of its neighbors, and translates directly into a node-specific depth: negative-curvature local hubs receive a deeper tree to reach far collaborative signals, positive-curvature peripheral nodes receive a shallower tree to avoid re-aggregating already-mixed signals, and curvature-flat nodes keep the standard depth. Because this scheme reduces to standard NGCF propagation when no node receives a curvature adjustment, NTCF provably contains NGCF as a special case while admitting a broader family of node-adaptive propagation patterns. 2. Preliminary 2.1. Tree-Structured View of GCF A useful but underexplored fact about Eq. 1 is that, from the standpoint of any single node v v , L L -layer GCN propagation produces an embedding that depends only on the rooted tree obtained by unrolling 𝒢 \mathcal{G} around v v to depth L L . We formalize this tree as follows. Definition 0 (Rooted Propagation Tree). For a node v ∈ 𝒱 v\in\mathcal{V} and depth L ∈ ℕ L\in\mathbb{N} , the rooted propagation tree 𝒯 v ( L ) \mathcal{T}_{v}^{(L)} is defined by breadth-first unrolling of 𝒢 \mathcal{G} from v v for L L hops. Each node in 𝒯 v ( L ) \mathcal{T}_{v}^{(L)} corresponds to a walk of length at most L L originating at v v , and edges follow the bipartite structure of 𝒢 \mathcal{G} . Under this view, GCN-style propagation can be equivalently described as: for every v ∈ 𝒱 v\in\mathcal{V} , build 𝒯 v ( L ) \mathcal{T}_{v}^{(L)} and aggregate information from leaves to root. This makes explicit the fact that NGCF and its successors implicitly assume the same tree depth L L for every node —a global hyper-parameter that ignores the heterogeneous local geometry of 𝒢 \mathcal{G} . We relax this assumption by allowing each node to have its own depth L v L_{v} , and we use a closed-form local-curvature score (Sec. 2.3 ) to determine L v L_{v} . 2.3. Conclusion In this paper, we revisit the structural assumptions of graph collaborative filtering and identify that fixing a global propagation depth ignores the heterogeneous local geometry of real user–item graphs. Motivated by this observation, we propose Neural Tree Collaborative Filtering (NTCF), which reinterprets each node’s neighborhood as a rooted tree and assigns a node-specific propagation depth based on a closed-form local-degree-imbalance curvature score. We theoretically prove that NTCF strictly generalizes NGCF, degenerating to NGCF in the zero-adjustment limit (lower bound), and that, under the same Lipschitz contraction assumption used to analyze over-smoothing, NTCF maintains a non-vanishing Dirichlet-energy floor that uniform-depth NGCF provably loses as L L grows. Extensive experiments on three real-world datasets verify that NTCF consistently outperforms widely used GCF backbones and further boosts state-of-the-art self-supervised recommenders when used as their backbone. We hope this motivates further work on geometry-aware, node-adaptive message-passing schedules for GCF. Acknowledgements.
